subject: Looping a T-test across multiple column containing values

messages.author: 4e113ea40ba2e533
messages.subject: Looping a T-test across multiple column containing values
parts:
Hi D-rug,

I am trying to write a loop to run a T-test comparing my 8 test subjects and 8 control subjects (16 total) for a very long list of protein/mass spec values.

Each protein is listed in the column name, with the first column representing the sampleID or group assignment. In this case I left group assignment as the first column, with messy protein names in the rest of the column names.

This is what my data looks like:



Do you know the best way to loop through this to perform a T-test for each set of values in a column, across all columns?

A friend helped come up with the following for loop:

for(i in 3:5726(df_t)) {
  newdf_name[i,1] = colnames(data[i])
  newdf_name[i,2] = t.test(data[1:8,i], data[9:16,i])
 
}

Any ideas would be fantastic. I haven't written a for-loop in many years.

Thank you!

messages.author: 27405c4b711a1080
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Looping a T-test across multiple column containing values
parts:
Nichole,

I've been trying hard to avoid for loops for a while now. So I tried to do the same here. 

library(broom)
library(tidyverse)

df_t <- tibble(Group = rep(c("Control", "Premutation"), each = 8), ID = c(1:8, 1:8), protein1 = rnorm(n= 16), protein2 = rnorm(n= 16), protein3 = rnorm(n= 16), protein4 = rnorm(n= 16))

df_t %>%
pivot_longer(., cols = -c(Group, ID)) %>%
nest(data = c(ID, Group, value)) %>%
mutate(
t_test = map(data, ~t.test(value ~ Group, data = .x)),
tidy_t = map(t_test, broom::tidy)
) %>%
unnest(tidy_t)

This gives you a table with the t.test performed per protein. I have no idea if this is the right test for your data, but hopefully this gets you further on your quest.

HTH,
Brandon

messages.author: 2226e6c311219eb7
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Re: Looping a T-test across multiple column containing values
parts:
Hi

I've only taken a quick look at the question, and while Brandon's solution may be useful in more complex situations,
I think you will be better served by a much simpler and more direct approach

  testResults = lapply(  data[, -1],   function(col)  t.test( col[1:8], col[9:16]))

or
   testResults = lapply(  data[, -1],   t.test, data[, 1])
 
The result is a list with as many elements as there are protein columns in your data.frame.
Each element is the result from t.test.  So, e.g.,
  sapply(testResults, function(x) x$p.value)
gets the p value from each test.

D.

parts: Have you considered multivariate analyses (e.g., NMDS, PCA, PLSDA, etc)? Regarding your approach, it seems like conducting so many tests in one experiment would increase the likelihood of making Type I errors.  There are various ways to correct for this (e.g., Bonferroni correction). Maybe someone more knowledgeable could provide guidelines for when and how to deal with this issue?
